name: GitHub (OAuth App)
summary: Register a GitHub OAuth App, send users through the authorization code flow with state and PKCE, and call the API on their behalf. Steps marked Authorization tested were exercised end to end on 2026-10-28 with a local loopback callback and no scopes.

wait.basis: The app worked immediately in two runs on 2026-10-28, and no GitHub page we checked describes a review before users can authorize an OAuth App.

effort.assumptions: an experienced developer, an existing web backend reachable over HTTPS with a secret store and a database for tokens, and a standard OAuth client library. Excludes organization approvals, security review and production rollout

prerequisites.text: A GitHub personal account, or admin access to the organization that will own the app.

source.quote: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to.

steps.title: Confirm an OAuth App is the right choice
steps.detail: GitHub recommends a GitHub App when you need narrower access. Pick an OAuth App only if its broader scope model is acceptable for your use case.

source.quote: GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions, give the user more control over which repositories the app can access, and use short-lived tokens.

time.basis: Reading GitHub's OAuth App vs GitHub App guidance and deciding.

steps.handoff: You choose; the agent can summarize the tradeoff.

steps.title: Register the OAuth App
steps.detail: Go to Settings → Developer settings → OAuth apps → New OAuth App (first-time accounts see “Register a new application”). Fill in the fields below and click Register application. Values shown are the ones we tested locally; replace them with your agent application's real URLs in production.

settings.explain: Shown to users on the consent screen. In production use your recognizable product name.
Local test only. Production: your agent application's public site, e.g. https://your-agent.example/ (illustrative, not tested).
Where GitHub sends the user back with the code. Local test only. Production: your backend's callback endpoint (illustrative, not tested). Up to 10 callback URLs are allowed.
Only for headless apps such as CLIs. Leave off for a web callback flow.

test_record.result: Registration succeeded and the app was used for the full flow below.
test_record.limits: Loopback callback on one machine; production URLs not tested.

source.quote: In "Authorization callback URL", type the callback URL of your app.

time.basis: Timed run: 37 s to fill and submit the form, with Claude driving Chrome. A person reading each field will be slower.

steps.handoff: Must happen in a browser signed in to the GitHub account that will own the app.

steps.title: Turn wildcard matching off unless you need it
steps.detail: Wildcard matching lets GitHub send codes to any subdomain or sub-path of your callback. GitHub's changelog says single-callback apps have it enabled, so check the setting after registering. Our test ran with it off.

source.quote: Apps with only one redirect URI have wildcard matching enabled.

time.basis: Checking one setting on the app page.

steps.title: Generate a client secret and store it server-side
steps.detail: On the app page, click Generate a new client secret. In our run GitHub asked for a Confirm access (sudo) check before showing it. Copy it straight into your backend's secret store; never put it in chat, URLs, logs or front-end code.

source.quote: Client secrets are required to generate access tokens for your app, unless your app uses the device flow.

time.basis: Timed run: 76 s including GitHub Confirm access by the account owner and moving the secret to a private file.

steps.handoff: GitHub asks for Confirm access (password, passkey or GitHub Mobile), which only the account owner can complete.

steps.title: Request only the scopes you need
steps.detail: Requesting no scope gives read-only access to public data, which is what we tested. Reading private repository contents needs the repo scope, which also grants write access; an OAuth App cannot narrow it to read-only.

source.quote: repo Grants full access to public and private repositories including read and write access to code

time.basis: Mapping the API calls you need to scopes on GitHub's scope list.

steps.handoff: You confirm which API calls your product needs.

steps.title: Send the user to GitHub with state and PKCE
steps.detail: Redirect to https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, an unguessable state and an S256 code_challenge. When the user returns, compare state before doing anything else.

test_record.result: Callback received; state matched; S256 PKCE used; no scopes requested.

source.quote: If the states don't match, then a third party created the request, and you should abort the process.

time.basis: Building the login redirect: state stored per session, PKCE verifier and challenge.

steps.handoff: You review, deploy, and keep the client secret in your secret store; a coding agent can write this part.

steps.title: Exchange the code for a token
steps.detail: POST client_id, client_secret, code, redirect_uri and code_verifier to the token endpoint with Accept: application/json.

test_record.result: HTTP 200; granted scopes empty; an expiring access token and a refresh token were returned.
test_record.limits: Token values were never printed or stored; refresh not exercised.

source.quote: Exchange this code for an access token: POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token

time.basis: Callback route, token exchange, and encrypted token storage.

steps.handoff: You review, deploy, and keep the client secret in your secret store; a coding agent can write this part.

steps.title: Call the API as the user
steps.detail: Send Authorization: Bearer <token>. We made exactly one read: GET https://api.github.com/user.

test_record.result: GET /user returned HTTP 200 with an empty X-OAuth-Scopes header.

source.quote: The access token allows you to make requests to the API on a behalf of a user.

time.basis: Wiring the token into your API client and handling 401 responses.

steps.handoff: You review, deploy, and keep the client secret in your secret store; a coding agent can write this part.

steps.title: Handle token expiry with refresh tokens
steps.detail: With expiring tokens on, store the refresh token securely and swap it for a new token pair before or after the access token expires.

source.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use.

time.basis: Refresh before or after expiry, storing the rotated refresh token, and re-auth on failure.

steps.handoff: You review, deploy, and keep the client secret in your secret store; a coding agent can write this part.

steps.title: Run one authorization end to end
steps.detail: With the pieces above in place, sign in once as a test user and make one read-only API call before building further.

time.basis: Timed run: 26 s from opening the authorize URL to a successful GET /user, including the consent click.

test_record.result: Second run on a fresh test app: state valid, S256 PKCE, token exchange HTTP 200, GET /user HTTP 200, no scopes.

source.quote: GitHub redirects back to your site with a temporary code in a code parameter

steps.handoff: A test user must click Authorize on GitHub's consent screen.

gaps.text: Token refresh and revocation were not exercised.
gaps.next_action: Run a refresh and a revoke against the test app.

gaps.text: Organization-owned apps and organization OAuth access restrictions were not researched.
gaps.next_action: Check GitHub docs on organization OAuth app access policies.

gaps.text: Production callback URLs were not tested; only a local loopback callback was.
gaps.next_action: Repeat the flow against a deployed callback.

verification.method: plain HTTPS fetch, tags stripped, normalized text match

difficulty.reason: No provider review before users can connect. The only human-only step is GitHub's Confirm access when you generate the client secret.
